module_title: Pickling and Preserving in Vinegar and Oil

lessons.title: Making Vinegar from Local Fruits
lessons.body: To make vinegar, you need a clean glass jar, a breathable cover like a cloth, and fruit scraps. Use overripe mangoes, pineapple peels, banana peels, or sugarcane juice. Chop fruits into small pieces. For every 1 kilogram of fruit, add 2 liters of clean water and 100 grams of sugar. Stir well. Pour into the jar, leaving 5 cm of space at the top. Cover with cloth and secure with a rubber band. Keep in a dark, warm place (25-30Â°C). Stir daily for the first week. After 2-3 weeks, you will see bubbles and smell alcohol. That is fermentation. Now strain the liquid into a new jar. Cover again and leave for 2-4 weeks. A thin film (mother of vinegar) may form. Taste after 3 weeks: it should be sour. If not, wait another week. Strain again and bottle. Store in a cool, dark place. It keeps for 6 months. For stronger vinegar, let it ferment longer. Use this vinegar for pickling. Do not use metal containers; use glass, ceramic, or food-grade plastic. Always label with date.

lessons.title: Pickling Vegetables: Onions, Cucumbers, Peppers
lessons.body: Start with fresh, firm vegetables. Wash and cut onions into rings, cucumbers into slices, peppers into strips. For a basic brine, mix 1 part vinegar (your homemade or bought) with 1 part water. Add 1 tablespoon of salt per liter of brine. For sweetness, add 1 tablespoon of sugar per liter. Bring brine to a boil, then cool. Pack vegetables tightly into clean glass jars. Add spices: mustard seeds, peppercorns, garlic cloves, or chili flakes. Pour cooled brine over vegetables, covering them completely. Leave 1 cm headspace. Seal jars with lids. For quick pickles, refrigerate and eat after 24 hours. For long-term storage, process jars in a hot water bath: place jars in a pot, cover with water, boil for 10 minutes. Remove and let cool. Check seals: lid should not pop when pressed. Store in a cool, dark place. Onions and peppers pickle in 1-2 weeks; cucumbers in 3-4 weeks. Always use clean jars and utensils. If you see mold, discard. For spicy pickles, add whole chilies.

lessons.title: Pickling Fish and Meat
lessons.body: Pickling fish and meat preserves them and adds flavor. Use fresh fish like tilapia or mackerel, or meat like beef or goat. Cut into small pieces (5 cm cubes). For fish, soak in salt water (100g salt per liter) for 1 hour. For meat, rub with salt and leave for 2 hours. Rinse well. Prepare a brine: 1 part vinegar, 1 part water, 1 tablespoon salt, 1 tablespoon sugar per liter. Add bay leaves, peppercorns, and garlic. Bring to a boil, then cool. Pack fish or meat into clean glass jars. Add sliced onions and carrots. Pour cooled brine over, covering completely. Leave 1 cm headspace. Seal and refrigerate. For fish, it is ready in 3-5 days. For meat, 7-10 days. Always keep refrigerated. For longer storage, you can process in a hot water bath for 20 minutes, but only if you are sure of acidity (pH below 4.6). Test with pH strips. If not, keep refrigerated and eat within 2 weeks. Never leave pickled fish or meat at room temperature. Discard if it smells bad or has mold.

lessons.title: Preserving in Oil: Garlic, Herbs, and Peppers
lessons.body: Preserving in oil is different from pickling. Oil does not kill bacteria; it blocks air. You must first dry or salt the food to remove moisture. For garlic: peel cloves, dry in sun for 2 days, then pack into jars. Cover with olive or sunflower oil. Add a pinch of salt. For herbs like basil or rosemary: wash, dry completely, chop, and pack into jars. Cover with oil. For peppers: roast or sun-dry, then pack in oil. Always use clean, dry jars. Any water can cause mold. Store in a cool, dark place. Use within 3 months. For safety, you can add 1 tablespoon of vinegar per cup of oil to increase acidity. Never store garlic in oil at room temperature for more than 1 week; keep refrigerated. Botulism risk is real. If you see bubbles, cloudiness, or bad smell, throw it away. For long-term, freeze the oil-preserved items in small containers. Always label with date. Use a clean spoon each time. Oil preservation is best for small batches. You can also mix oil and vinegar for a vinaigrette style.

lessons.title: Balancing Acidity and Flavor
lessons.body: The key to safe pickles is acidity. The pH must be below 4.6. You can buy pH strips from pharmacies or agricultural supply shops. Test your brine before pouring. If pH is too high, add more vinegar. A simple rule: use at least 1 part vinegar to 1 part water. For stronger pickles, use 2 parts vinegar to 1 part water. Vinegar should be at least 5% acetic acid. If yours is weaker, use more. Flavor balance: taste the brine. It should be sour, salty, and slightly sweet. Adjust with sugar, salt, or spices. For African flavors, add chili, ginger, garlic, or local herbs like scent leaf or coriander. Do not reduce salt; it helps preserve. Do not add oil to vinegar pickles; it can cause spoilage. For oil-preserved items, add a little vinegar for safety. Always write down your recipe so you can repeat it. Keep a notebook. Test each batch with pH strips. If you sell, your customers trust you. Safe pickles last longer and taste better. Remember: if in doubt, throw it out.

lessons.title: Packaging and Selling Pickled Products
lessons.body: To sell pickles, you need attractive, safe packaging. Use clean glass jars with metal lids. New lids are best; they seal properly. Wash jars in hot soapy water, rinse, and dry in oven at 100Â°C for 10 minutes. Fill jars with pickles, leaving 1 cm headspace. Wipe rims, seal. Label with product name, ingredients, date, and your contact. For local markets, use small jars (250 ml) for affordability. Price: calculate cost of ingredients, jars, labels, and your time. Add 30-50% profit. For example, if a jar costs 500 CFA to make, sell at 800-1000 CFA. Sell at markets, shops, or online. Offer samples. Keep records of sales and expenses. For transport, pack jars in boxes with newspaper to prevent breakage. Store in cool, dark place. Do not sell if seal is broken or mold appears. Get a food handling certificate if required. Build a brand: use a simple logo and consistent recipes. Ask customers for feedback. Repeat buyers are key. You can also sell in bulk to restaurants. Always follow local health regulations.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Pickling and Preserving in Vinegar and Oil

Pickling is one of the highest-margin food preservation businesses available to small-scale African processors. A 20-litre bucket of cucumbers bought at farm gate for the equivalent of US$8â12 can become 40â55 retail jars selling at US$1.50â3.00 each in urban markets, supermarkets, and to diaspora buyers. The chemistry is simple, the equipment is cheap, and the shelf life â when done correctly â runs from 6 to 24 months without refrigeration. This lesson gives you the practical numbers, ratios, and process controls you need to pickle safely and sell profitably.

1. Making Vinegar from Local Fruits

Commercial white vinegar (5% acetic acid) is the safest base for pickling, but in many African markets it is expensive or inconsistently available. You can produce your own vinegar from banana, pineapple, mango, palm wine, or sorghum beer using a two-stage fermentation: alcoholic fermentation by yeast, then acetic acid fermentation by Acetobacter bacteria.

Process: Mash ripe fruit with water (1:2 by weight), add 5â10% sugar if the fruit is low in sugar, and ferment in a covered bucket for 5â10 days until bubbling stops (alcohol stage). Strain, then expose the liquid to air in a wide-mouthed container covered with cloth. Acetobacter converts alcohol to acetic acid over 2â4 weeks. Test acidity with a titration kit or pH meter; target 4â5% acetic acid for pickling. Homemade vinegar below 4% is unsafe for shelf-stable pickles â use it only for refrigerator pickles or blend it with commercial vinegar.

2. Pickling Vegetables: Onions, Cucumbers, Peppers

Vegetable pickling is the fastest route to revenue because the raw material is cheap and the process takes 24â72 hours. The key control is brine strength. Use a 1:1 ratio of vinegar to water for shelf-stable pickles, plus 2â3% salt by weight of the total liquid. For a 5-litre batch: 2.5 L vinegar (5%), 2.5 L water, 150 g non-iodised salt, 100 g sugar, spices.

Process: Wash vegetables, cut to uniform size, blanch cucumbers and peppers for 30â60 seconds (onions need no blanching). Pack hot, sterilised jars tightly, pour hot brine (85â90Â°C) to within 1 cm of the rim, remove air bubbles, seal, and process in a water bath at 90Â°C for 10â15 minutes. Cool, label, and store in a dark place.

Table 1: Brine Formulations for Common African Pickled Vegetables (per 1 litre finished brine)
Vegetable Vinegar (5%) Water Salt Sugar Processing Time Shelf Life (sealed)
Cucumbers (gherkins)500 ml500 ml30 g20 g15 min12â18 months
Onions (pearl)600 ml400 ml25 g30 g10 min12 months
Peppers (whole)500 ml500 ml30 g15 g15 min12â24 months
Mixed vegetables550 ml450 ml28 g25 g15 min12 months

Source: Adapted from FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius, Standard for Pickled Fruits and Vegetables (CODEX STAN 260-2007) and Tanzania Bureau of Standards TZS 574:2016.

3. Pickling Fish and Meat

Fish and meat pickling is higher-value but higher-risk. In West Africa, "pickled fish" (often tilapia or mackerel) sells at 2â3Ã the price of fresh fish in urban markets. The acid must penetrate the flesh; use a 1:1 vinegar-to-water brine with 5% salt and refrigerate during the 48â72 hour curing step. After curing, pack in fresh brine or oil and process.

Critical control: Never pickle fish or meat that has been at ambient temperature for more than 2 hours. Use only fresh or properly frozen-then-thawed product. The finished product must reach a pH of 4.6 or below throughout â test the thickest part with a calibrated pH meter.

4. Preserving in Oil: Garlic, Herbs, and Peppers

Oil preservation is popular but is the most dangerous method if done incorrectly. Clostridium botulinum and Listeria can survive in oil because oil excludes oxygen but does not stop anaerobic bacteria. Garlic-in-oil is a known botulism risk worldwide.

â  SAFETY WARNING â OIL PRESERVATION: Never store raw garlic, herbs, or peppers in oil at room temperature. Garlic and herbs must first be acidified (soaked in vinegar for at least 24 hours) or dried to below 10% moisture before covering with oil. All oil-preserved products must be refrigerated and consumed within 2 weeks, or pressure-canned for shelf stability. Discard any oil preserve showing bubbles, cloudiness, or a sour smell. Botulism is odourless and can be fatal.

Safe method: Acidify garlic cloves in vinegar for 24â48 hours, drain, then cover with hot (80Â°C) oil, seal, and refrigerate. For shelf-stable herb oils, dry herbs fully, infuse in oil at 60Â°C for 2 hours, strain, and bottle. Label clearly: "Keep refrigerated. Use within 14 days."

5. Balancing Acidity and Flavor

Flavour balance determines repeat sales. The target profile is: acid (vinegar) 40â60%, sweet (sugar or honey) 20â30%, salt 10â15%, spice/aroma 5â10%. Adjust to local taste â East African markets prefer sweeter pickles; West African markets prefer hotter, saltier profiles.

Table 2: Flavour Balance Guide by Regional Market (percentage of total brine weight)
Market Vinegar Sugar Salt Chilli/Spice Typical pH
East Africa (Kenya, Tanzania)45%30%15%10%3.6â3.9
West Africa (Nigeria, Ghana)50%15%20%15%3.4â3.7
Southern Africa55%20%15%10%3.3â3.6
Diaspora export50%25%15%10%3.5â3.8

Source: Compiled from ITC Africa Market Access Survey (2021) and African Orphan Crops Consortium consumer preference data (2020).

6. Packaging and Selling Pickled Products

Packaging drives price. A glass jar with a printed label sells for 40â70% more than the same product in a reused plastic container. Invest in: food-grade glass jars with metal lug or twist-off caps, waterproof labels with product name, ingredients, net weight, best-before date, batch number, and producer contact. In most African countries, you need a business licence, a food handling certificate, and compliance with the national standards body (KEBS, NAFDAC, TBS, Ghana FDA, etc.).

Unit economics (typical 250 ml jar): Ingredients US$0.35, jar and cap US$0.30, label US$0.05, labour and overhead US$0.15 = US$0.85 cost. Wholesale US$1.60, retail US$2.50â3.00. Gross margin 47â65%. A one-person operation producing 100 jars/day can generate US$80â150 daily gross profit.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Test vinegar acidity â minimum 4% acetic acid for shelf-stable pickles.
  2. Use non-iodised salt; iodine causes darkening and softening.
  3. Sterilise jars and lids in boiling water for 10 minutes before filling.
  4. Fill jars to within 1 cm of the rim; remove all air bubbles.
  5. Process sealed jars in a 90Â°C water bath for 10â15 minutes.
  6. Check pH of finished product â target 4.6 or below throughout.
  7. Label every jar with batch number and best-before date.
  8. Store in a cool, dark place; refrigerate after opening.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Small-Scale Food Processing: Vinegar and Pickles (free)
  • FAO â Fruits and Vegetables Processing Toolkit (free)
  • Codex Alimentarius â Standards for Pickled Products (free)
  • CDC â Botulism Prevention in Home and Small-Scale Food Preservation (free)
  • International Trade Centre â Market Access for African Agro-Processed Products (free)

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of using a cloth cover during vinegar fermentation?
options: B) To allow air in while keeping dust out
quiz.explanation: A cloth cover allows oxygen in for acetic acid bacteria while blocking dust and insects.

quiz.q: How much sugar is added per kilogram of fruit when making vinegar?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states to add 100 grams of sugar per kilogram of fruit.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for fermenting vinegar?
quiz.explanation: The lesson recommends a dark, warm place at 25-30Â°C.

quiz.q: How long should you wait before straining the liquid after the first fermentation?
quiz.explanation: After 2-3 weeks, you see bubbles and smell alcohol, then you strain.

quiz.q: What is the 'mother of vinegar'?
options: B) A thin film that forms on top
quiz.explanation: The lesson describes a thin film (mother of vinegar) that may form.

quiz.q: Which container should you avoid when making vinegar?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says do not use metal containers; use glass, ceramic, or food-grade plastic.

quiz.q: For basic pickling brine, what is the ratio of vinegar to water?
quiz.explanation: The lesson uses 1 part vinegar to 1 part water.

quiz.q: How much salt is added per liter of brine for pickling vegetables?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says add 1 tablespoon of salt per liter of brine.

quiz.q: How long should you process jars in a hot water bath for long-term storage?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states to boil jars for 10 minutes.

quiz.q: How do you check if a jar is sealed properly?
options: B) Press the lid; it should not pop
quiz.explanation: The lesson says the lid should not pop when pressed.

quiz.q: How long do cucumber pickles take to be ready?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says cucumbers pickle in 3-4 weeks.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see mold on pickled vegetables?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says if you see mold, discard.

quiz.q: For pickling fish, how long should you soak it in salt water?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says soak fish in salt water for 1 hour.

quiz.q: How long should you rub salt on meat for pickling?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says rub meat with salt and leave for 2 hours.

quiz.q: How long does pickled fish take to be ready in the refrigerator?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says fish is ready in 3-5 days.

quiz.q: What is the maximum pH for safe pickling?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states pH must be below 4.6.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid storing garlic in oil at room temperature for more than a week?
quiz.explanation: The lesson warns of botulism risk; keep refrigerated.

quiz.q: What should you add to oil-preserved items to increase safety?
quiz.explanation: The lesson suggests adding 1 tablespoon of vinegar per cup of oil.

quiz.q: What is the minimum acetic acid concentration for vinegar used in pickling?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says vinegar should be at least 5% acetic acid.

quiz.q: How can you test the acidity of your brine?
quiz.explanation: The lesson recommends pH strips from pharmacies or agricultural shops.

quiz.q: What is a good practice when developing a pickle recipe?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says always write down your recipe so you can repeat it.

quiz.q: What should you do if you are in doubt about the safety of a pickle?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says: if in doubt, throw it out.

quiz.q: What type of jar is best for selling pickles?
options: B) Glass jars with metal lids
quiz.explanation: The lesson recommends clean glass jars with metal lids.

quiz.q: How much headspace should be left when filling pickle jars?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says leave 1 cm headspace.

quiz.q: What should be included on a pickle label?
options: B) Product name, ingredients, date, contact
quiz.explanation: The lesson says label with product name, ingredients, date, and contact.

quiz.q: How can you determine the selling price of your pickles?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says calculate cost and add 30-50% profit.

quiz.q: What is a good way to prevent jar breakage during transport?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says pack jars in boxes with newspaper.

quiz.q: Why is it important to get a food handling certificate?
options: A) It is required by law in some places
C) It makes jars seal better
quiz.explanation: The lesson says get a food handling certificate if required.

quiz.q: What is a key to building a successful pickle brand?
options: B) Consistent recipes and simple logo
quiz.explanation: The lesson says build a brand with simple logo and consistent recipes.

quiz.q: What should you do if a jar seal is broken before selling?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says do not sell if seal is broken or mold appears.
